title: Read-Only Objects
summary: Design tamper-proof immutable data structures by omitting setters and providing initialized read-only properties.
learningOutcomes: Create read-only objects using private fields and getter-only access
Understand why immutability eliminates concurrency bugs and side-effect mutations
Initialize all state exclusively via the constructor at object birth

activities.title: Everyday Analogy: The Museum Glass Display Case

analogy.story:
When you visit a history museum to view ancient gold artifacts or an original constitution document, it is placed behind bulletproof glass.

You can look closely at it, read every word, take photographs, and show your friends (Read access / Getter). But there is no slot, knob, or drawer for you to reach in with a pen and scribble corrections or rearrange the pages (No Write access / No Setter).

A read-only object in Java is that museum display case: it is fully observable by the world, but impossible to modify once sealed by the constructor.
analogy.takeaway: Omitting setters creates read-only objects. Once born via the constructor, their state is locked forever, making them immune to accidental tampering.

activities.title: Read-Only Design and Immutability Benefits

concept.explanation:
In software development, objects that can be freely mutated at any time by different parts of an application are a major source of elusive bugs (called 'action at a distance'). If Component A passes an object to Component B, and Component B secretly modifies a field, Component A will subsequently behave unpredictably.

How to design a Read-Only Object:
1. All fields are marked private.
2. All fields are initialized once during constructor execution.
3. Only getter methods are exposed; absolutely no setter methods are provided.
4. If fields contain primitive values (int, double, boolean) or immutable objects (String), the object is completely tamper-proof.

Benefits:
- Thread-Safety: Multiple threads can read simultaneously without data race conditions.
- Predictability: You can pass the object into third-party libraries knowing it cannot be altered.
- Cacheability: Hash codes and calculated representations can be safely cached.
rules: Rule 1: Never provide a setter on a read-only object.
Rule 2: Pass all required data into the constructor at creation time.
Rule 3: Read-only objects are inherently safe to share across multiple classes.

keyTakeaways: Rule 1: Never provide a setter on a read-only object.
Rule 2: Pass all required data into the constructor at creation time.
Rule 3: Read-only objects are inherently safe to share across multiple classes.

questions.prompt: How do you design a read-only property in a Java class using encapsulation?
questions.question: How do you design a read-only property in a Java class using encapsulation?
options: Mark the field public static
Make the field private and provide a public getter, but provide NO setter
Declare the class as abstract
Use a while loop inside the constructor
questions.explanation: A private field with a getter and no setter allows the value to be inspected but never modified after construction.

questions.prompt: When is the state of a read-only object assigned?
questions.question: When is the state of a read-only object assigned?
options: At runtime whenever the garbage collector runs
Exclusively during constructor execution at object birth
Whenever a getter is invoked
During class compilation
questions.explanation: Read-only objects receive all their initial data through constructor parameters at instantiation time.

questions.prompt: What is 'action at a distance' bug in software engineering?
questions.question: What is 'action at a distance' bug in software engineering?
options: A bug caused by slow internet connections
A bug where passing a mutable object to another method causes that method to unexpectedly alter the object's state, corrupting the caller's logic
A syntax error in remote Java servers
A memory leak in the JVM
questions.explanation: Action at a distance occurs when mutable shared objects are altered unexpectedly by external components.

questions.prompt: Why are read-only objects inherently thread-safe?
questions.question: Why are read-only objects inherently thread-safe?
options: Because the CPU automatically stops all other threads
Because their state never changes after construction, so concurrent reader threads can never observe conflicting writes
Because Java duplicates the object for every thread
Because they do not allocate heap memory
questions.explanation: Thread-safety issues arise from concurrent writes; if an object is read-only, writers do not exist, eliminating race conditions.

questions.prompt: Which standard Java class is a famous example of an immutable read-only object?
questions.question: Which standard Java class is a famous example of an immutable read-only object?
options: java.lang.String
java.util.ArrayList
java.lang.StringBuilder
java.util.Scanner
questions.explanation: String in Java is completely immutable; once created, its character contents can never be changed.

questions.prompt: Can a class have some fields that are read-only and other fields that are mutable?
questions.question: Can a class have some fields that are read-only and other fields that are mutable?
options: No, a class must be 100% mutable or 100% read-only
Yes, by providing setters only for the mutable fields and omitting setters for the read-only fields
Only if the read-only fields are static
Only if the class has two constructors
questions.explanation: Selective encapsulation allows permanent fields (like ID or PAN) to be read-only while dynamic fields (like address) remain mutable.

questions.prompt: If you need to change the data represented by a read-only object, what is the standard idiomatic OOP pattern?
questions.question: If you need to change the data represented by a read-only object, what is the standard idiomatic OOP pattern?
options: Use reflection to force overwrite private fields
Instantiate a new object with the updated values
Call the destructor and recreate the heap
Set the object reference to 0
questions.explanation: With immutable objects, modifications produce a fresh new object holding the revised values (just like String.replace() does).

questions.prompt: In our museum analogy, what represents the absence of setters?
questions.question: In our museum analogy, what represents the absence of setters?
options: The museum ticket counter
The sealed glass case with no opening for visitors to reach inside
The museum gift shop
The security guards walking outside
questions.explanation: The sealed glass case represents private fields exposed via getters only with no setters.

questions.prompt: Why are database primary keys and transaction IDs almost always modeled as read-only fields?
questions.question: Why are database primary keys and transaction IDs almost always modeled as read-only fields?
options: Because changing identity keys breaks data integrity and relational mapping across systems
Because Java integers cannot be changed once created
Because databases reject objects with setters
To reduce disk space
questions.explanation: Identity keys must never change once assigned; changing an entity's ID corrupts logs, relations, and caches.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to ensure an object's read-only fields are never left uninitialized or null?
questions.question: What is the best way to ensure an object's read-only fields are never left uninitialized or null?
options: Provide a no-arg constructor that does nothing
Require all mandatory read-only fields as parameters in the constructor and validate them
Set all fields to public
Declare fields as static
questions.explanation: Requiring all read-only fields as constructor parameters guarantees that every instance is fully and validly populated at creation.

questions.question: How do you implement a read-only or immutable object in Java without using the 'final' keyword?
questions.answer: Make all instance variables private, initialize them completely through constructor arguments, and provide only getter methods without providing any setters or state-modifying methods. (Adding 'final' is a best practice we study in Module 4, but encapsulation alone establishes read-only access).
keyTakeaways: Private fields + Constructor initialization + Getters only = Read-only

questions.question: What are the primary architectural benefits of immutability in enterprise backends?
questions.answer: 1. Thread safety with zero synchronization overhead. 2. Failure atomicity (an immutable object never exists in a corrupt intermediate state). 3. Safe sharing as Map keys or Cache entries without fear of hashcode alteration.

questions.question: What is the Copy-on-Write (or functional update) pattern?
questions.answer: Instead of mutating an existing object, a method returns a brand new instance containing the altered value while leaving the original instance untouched. A classic example is 'String s2 = s1.toUpperCase();'.
keyTakeaways: Returns new instance instead of modifying current

questions.question: Why is an immutable object safer as a HashMap key than a mutable object?
questions.answer: A HashMap calculates a bucket location using the key's hashCode(). If the key is mutable and its fields change after being placed in the map, its hashCode changes, making it impossible to locate or retrieve the key from the map later.
keyTakeaways: Mutable keys break HashMap hash contracts
Immutable keys guarantee stable hash codes

questions.question: Can a class with only getters still be accidentally mutable?
questions.answer: Yes! If a getter returns a direct reference to a mutable internal object (such as a Date or an int[] array), external code can mutate the contents through that reference even without a setter. Defensive copies are required for mutable field types.

questions.question: When would you prefer a mutable object over a read-only object?
questions.answer: When frequent, high-volume state modifications occur in performance-critical loops (e.g., appending characters in StringBuilder or updating high-frequency gaming coordinates) where creating millions of short-lived objects would cause excessive garbage collection pressure.
keyTakeaways: Avoid GC pressure in hot loops

Print 'Ticket XYZ889 for Deepak: Seat 14C'.

practiceProblems.title: Challenge: Functional Copy-on-Write Color Palette
practiceProblems.description: Write a complete ReadOnlyColor class from scratch with private int red, private int green, private int blue (0 to 255). Provide a constructor setting all 3 (clamp 0-255). Provide only getters. Provide a functional method withRed(int newRed) that does NOT mutate this object, but returns a BRAND NEW ReadOnlyColor instance with updated red and the same green and blue. In Main, create color (100, 150, 200), call withRed(255) into a new variable, and print 'Original: 100, 150, 200 | Revised: 255, 150, 200'.
